cards.front: PPH is blood loss ≥[___] mL after vaginal birth (≥1000 mL after CS); primary = within 24 hours of birth, secondary = beyond that up to 6 weeks postpartum.
cards.context:
The 500 mL threshold for vaginal birth (1000 mL after CS) is a clinical convention, not a physiological cutoff — most women tolerate 500 mL without compromise because of the pregnancy-induced 50% rise in blood volume.

Temporal split: PRIMARY PPH within 24 h (most within 1 h, dominant cause uterine atony — apply 4 Ts); SECONDARY PPH from 24 h to 6 weeks (most in 2nd week, dominant causes retained products and endometritis).

cards.front: Neonatal resuscitation adrenaline (HR persistently <[___] despite PPV + compressions): 0.1-0.3 mL/kg of 1:10,000 IV via umbilical venous catheter (UVC).
cards.context:
Adrenaline in neonatal resus is reserved for persistent HR <60 despite effective PPV + chest compressions for ≥30 sec.

Ventilation remains the priority — adrenaline without effective ventilation is futile in respiratory-arrest physiology.

Volume expansion (10 mL/kg saline) for hypovolaemia; glucose only if confirmed hypoglycaemia.

cards.front: Preconception planning should begin [___] months before conception; the five pillars include folate, lifestyle, medication review, chronic disease control, and reproductive carrier screening.
cards.context:
The 3-6 month window matters because highest-risk fetal development precedes a recognised pregnancy. The neural tube closes by day 28 and organogenesis is done by 12 weeks, so optimisation must precede conception.

Five pillars: folate; lifestyle (smoking, alcohol, weight); medication review (switch teratogens: warfarin, ACEi/ARB, methotrexate, isotretinoin); carrier screening (identify carrier couples early).

Plus chronic disease control: diabetes, epilepsy, SLE and thyroid stable BEFORE conception, when first-trimester glycaemia and disease activity set anomaly and miscarriage risk.

cards.front: Pre-eclampsia diagnosis requires hypertension after 20 weeks PLUS new [___] involvement (renal, hepatic, haematological, neurological, pulmonary, or placental).
cards.context:
2018 ISSHP/SOMANZ broadened pre-eclampsia from 'HTN + proteinuria' to 'HTN + ANY new organ involvement' — ~20% of pre-eclampsia has no significant proteinuria but still has organ dysfunction.

Organ systems to screen at every visit after 20 weeks: renal (urinalysis, creatinine), hepatic (LFTs), haematological (FBC, haemolysis film), neurological (visual, headache, hyperreflexia), pulmonary (oedema, dyspnoea).

cards.front: PCOS Rotterdam criteria require [___] of 3: oligo/anovulation, hyperandrogenism (clinical or biochemical), and polycystic ovaries on USS.
cards.context:
PCOS = 2 of 3 Rotterdam criteria: oligo/anovulation, hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne, alopecia, OR raised free testosterone), polycystic ovaries on USS (≥20 follicles per ovary or volume >10 mL).

Downstream risks: endometrial hyperplasia + cancer from unopposed oestrogen (cyclic progestogen if anovulatory), insulin resistance + T2DM, CV disease, and subfertility (letrozole first-line).

Assess glycaemic status at diagnosis and repeat every 1-3 years according to diabetes risk. A 75-g OGTT is the most accurate test; fasting glucose or HbA1c are less accurate alternatives when an OGTT cannot be performed.

cards.front: Complete molar pregnancy is karyotype 46,XX (paternal/androgenetic); partial mole is [___]; ~15-20% of complete moles progress to GTN.
cards.context:
Complete mole: empty ovum + sperm that duplicates (46,XX paternal) or two sperm (46,XY paternal) — no fetal tissue, diffuse villous oedema, very high βhCG, 15-20% progress to GTN.

Partial mole: normal ovum + two sperm — triploid, most commonly 69,XXY (dispermic fertilisation of an X-bearing ovum.

69,XXX and 69,XYY occur less often) — abnormal fetal tissue, focal villous oedema, moderate βhCG, ~1-5% malignant risk.

cards.front: The newborn bloodspot screens for treatable conditions including PKU, congenital hypothyroidism, and cystic [___].
cards.context:
The newborn bloodspot ('heel-prick' / Guthrie) screens around day 2–3 for treatable conditions where early detection prevents serious harm.

Examples: PKU, congenital hypothyroidism, cystic fibrosis, and several metabolic disorders.

cards.front: Vitamin K prophylaxis: preferred IM dose 1 mg at birth; if declined, oral regimen is [___] doses over 4 weeks.
cards.context:
VKDB (formerly HDN) affects neonates because the liver doesn't synthesise factors II, VII, IX, X without vitamin K, and breast milk has minimal vitamin K.

IM vitamin K 1 mg at birth — single-dose, near-100% effective, no compliance issues.

cards.front: The ideal fetal presentation is flexed vertex, occiput [___]; the smallest presenting diameter is the suboccipitobregmatic (~9.5 cm).
cards.context:
The fetal head is not a sphere — different presenting diameters depend on degree of flexion and orientation.

Deflexed heads (military, brow, face) present larger diameters (~11-13 cm) that may not fit → obstructed labour.

Occiput posterior (OP) babies present a slightly larger diameter (~10 cm) AND face the wrong way for the pelvic curve → prolonged labour + 'back labour'.

cards.front: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (PPROM) occurs between 20+0 and 36+6 weeks; diagnose with history plus sterile [___] examination, avoiding digital examination unless active labour or birth is imminent.
cards.context:
PPROM means membrane rupture before labour and before 37 weeks; PROM is prelabour rupture at term, while SROM occurs after labour starts.

Diagnose from a history of a gush or persistent leaking, confirmed by sterile speculum examination.

Avoid digital examination unless active labour is established or birth is imminent, because it can introduce vaginal flora and shorten latency.

cards.front: Conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinaemia in a neonate is never normal — exclude biliary [___].
cards.context:
The reason any newborn jaundice with a raised CONJUGATED fraction is a red flag: it's never physiological.

The key surgical cause to exclude early is biliary atresia, where the Kasai procedure works only if done in the first weeks.

cards.front: Hypertension in pregnancy is SBP ≥140 and/or DBP ≥[___] mmHg on 2 occasions ≥4 h apart (or a single reading ≥160/110).
cards.context:
The pregnancy threshold (140/90) sits below the general adult treatment threshold because mild hypertension matters more here.

Placental perfusion is pressure-dependent, and untreated HTN drives pre-eclampsia, abruption, and IUGR.

Timing reframes the same number. Before 20 weeks, 140/90 is chronic HTN (secondary-cause workup); after 20 weeks it is gestational HTN or pre-eclampsia, triggering an end-organ screen (urinalysis, LFTs, FBC, creatinine).

cards.front: A complete hydatidiform mole is most often karyotype 46,XX with entirely paternal genetic origin. No fetal tissue is present; malignant risk is [___]%.
cards.context:
Complete mole: empty ovum fertilised by sperm that duplicates its DNA; most are 46,XX and entirely paternal, with no fetal tissue.

Compared with partial mole, complete mole has higher βhCG and malignant risk. Manage with suction curette, then βhCG surveillance; plateau or rise means persistent GTN.

cards.front: [___] syndrome is a severe pre-eclampsia variant defined by a microangiopathic blood-film picture, raised transaminases, and thrombocytopenia.
cards.context:
HELLP is a severe pre-eclampsia variant, but ~15% occur WITHOUT classic pre-eclampsia features (normotensive HELLP) — diagnosis depends on the lab triad: haemolysis (LDH >600, schistocytes, indirect bilirubin).

Rapid progression: hepatic subcapsular haematoma + rupture, DIC + haemorrhage, AKI, pulmonary oedema, eclamptic seizure, abruption. Maternal mortality 1-3%, perinatal 10-30%.

Management is delivery at any gestation if maternal status deteriorating; steroids for fetal maturity if time permits; Mg for seizure prophylaxis even without prior eclampsia.

cards.front: Suspected chorioamnionitis: give [___] antibiotics and plan delivery — do not prolong pregnancy.
cards.context:
Chorioamnionitis (intra-amniotic infection) is bacterial colonisation of fetal membranes, amniotic fluid, and placenta — typically ascending after ROM.

Delivery is part of source control — leaving an infected uterus prolongs sepsis and worsens neonatal outcomes.

Empirical IV antibiotics (amoxicillin/clindamycin + gentamicin, or piperacillin-tazobactam) + delivery; vaginal if labour progressing, CS if obstetric indication.

cards.front: Hyperemesis gravidarum causes severe nausea and/or vomiting beginning before [___] weeks, preventing normal oral intake and strongly limiting daily activities.
cards.context:
The Windsor definition is severe nausea or vomiting before 16 weeks, inability to eat or drink normally, and strong limitation of daily activities. Ketonuria is neither required nor a severity marker.

Treat dehydration with IV 0.9% saline, potassium guided by electrolytes, and antiemetics. Consider thromboprophylaxis; reserve parenteral nutrition for severe refractory cases.

cards.front: Cord prolapse: position the patient in [___] or knee-chest and elevate the presenting part; if vaginal birth is not imminent, expedite caesarean birth.
cards.context:
Cord prolapse can rapidly compromise fetal oxygenation. Immediately use steep Trendelenburg or knee-chest and manually elevate the presenting part.

If vaginal birth is not imminent, expedite caesarean birth: category 1 for a suspicious or pathological fetal heart rate; category 2 may be considered with a normal trace.

For prolonged transfer, bladder filling with 500-750 mL saline can maintain elevation. Minimise cord handling to avoid vasospasm.

cards.front: Active neonatal resuscitation: not routinely recommended <[___] weeks; offered at family discretion in the borderline window; recommended ≥25 weeks.
cards.context:
Thresholds for active resuscitation reflect survival + disability outcomes at each gestation. Below 23 weeks: virtually no survivors with intact neurology (palliative comfort care).

At 23 weeks: very low survival (~30-40% at best, many with moderate-severe disability) — individualised decision; at 24 weeks: ~50-70% survival.
